title_alt: You're Surrounded at Bastogne. The Germans Want You to Surrender.

hook_description: December 1944. The 101st Airborne is surrounded at Bastogne, freezing in foxholes without winter coats and nearly out of ammunition, when the Germans send a letter demanding surrender. Joe, a 19-year-old paratrooper, tells how they held on until the day after Christmas.

scenes.title: Surrender
scenes.narration: December 22nd, 1944. We're surrounded in the frozen woods of Belgium. And the Germans just walked up to our line under a white flag with a letter. Surrender or be destroyed.

scenes.title: Eight days
scenes.narration: Our general answered with one word. I'll tell you what it was. But first, let me show you how we got there and how we held that town, with no winter coats and almost no ammunition, until the day after Christmas.

scenes.title: A week earlier
scenes.narration: A week before, we were resting in France. We'd jumped into Holland in September, and we were waiting for new boots, new coats, new men. Then, on December 16th, the Germans smashed through the Ardennes forest. The army needed someone fast. They sent us.

scenes.title: Who I am
scenes.narration: My name's Joe Novak. I'm nineteen, a private in the 101st Airborne. Back home in Pittsburgh, I worked in my uncle's butcher shop. I'd made one combat jump. I thought I knew what war was. I didn't know anything about winter.

scenes.title: The trucks
scenes.narration: They packed us standing up into open trucks and drove us all night through the cold, headlights on. No winter coats. Most of us had only a few clips of ammunition. We didn't even know where we were going until somebody saw a sign. Bastogne.

scenes.title: The wrong way
scenes.narration: As we marched in, other soldiers were streaming out the other way. Tired, scared, some without weapons. We asked them for their ammunition, their grenades, anything. They handed it over and kept walking. One of them looked at me and said: you're going the wrong way.

scenes.title: Into the town
scenes.narration: Bastogne was a small market town, with seven roads running out of it like the spokes of a wheel. That's why both armies wanted it. Whoever held those roads held the whole region. The townspeople watched us march in from their doorways then went down into their cellars.

scenes.title: Frozen ground
scenes.narration: They put us in a ring of woods and fields around the town. The ground was frozen like rock. We chipped our foxholes with little shovels, and lined the bottom with pine branches, so we weren't lying in the snow. Lenny and I shared one hole for the next week.

scenes.title: Lenny
scenes.narration: Lenny Hart, from Texas. He'd never seen snow before the army. He talked the whole time about his girl, about chili, about the garage he was going to open after the war. When you're freezing in a hole, a guy who never stops talking is the best thing in the world.

scenes.title: Surrounded
scenes.narration: On December 20th, the last road out was cut. By the next morning, we were completely surrounded. Somebody in our company shrugged and said: they've got us surrounded the poor bastards.

scenes.title: The cold
scenes.narration: Then came the cold. One of the coldest winters that part of Europe had seen in years. At night, it fell far below freezing. Our canteens froze solid. We slept sitting up, back to back, one blanket over both of us.

scenes.title: Our feet
scenes.narration: The real enemy was our feet. Wet boots, no dry socks, no way to warm up. Trench foot. Your toes went white, then numb. Every few hours, Lenny and I took turns pulling off each other's boots and rubbing our feet, just to keep the blood moving.

scenes.narration: On the snow, we were dark green targets. So the people of Bastogne gave us their bedsheets, their tablecloths, even their curtains. We wrapped them over our helmets and coats. From fifty yards away, you could hardly see us.

scenes.title: Patrol in the fog
scenes.narration: At night we went out on patrol, three or four of us, into the fog. You couldn't see ten feet. You listened. A cough. A canteen clinking. A branch snapping. Half the time, you didn't know if the shape ahead of you was one of ours or one of theirs.

scenes.narration: Thousands of Belgian families were trapped in the town with us, hiding in their cellars. One woman, Marie, carried soup out to our foxholes in a milk can. I never knew her last name. I never forgot that soup.

scenes.narration: We were running out of everything. Our artillery was told to fire only when an attack was coming. The medics ran short of bandages and blankets. And low clouds and fog kept every plane on the ground. Nothing could reach us.

scenes.narration: He read it and said one word. Nuts. That became his official reply. When the German officer asked what it meant, our colonel told him: it means, go to hell. When that word came down the line, we laughed for the first time in days.

scenes.title: Parachutes
scenes.narration: Cargo planes came in low, and the sky filled with parachutes. Red, yellow, blue each color meant something: ammunition, food, medicine. Guys climbed out of their holes and cheered, waving at the pilots like kids at a parade.

scenes.title: Christmas Eve
scenes.narration: On Christmas Eve, the general sent a message to every man. What's merry about all this, he asked? And he answered: we have stopped cold everything that has been thrown at us. That night, enemy planes bombed the town. In our hole, Lenny sang Silent Night very quietly.

scenes.title: Christmas morning
scenes.narration: At dawn on Christmas Day, they hit us hard, with tanks painted white and infantry behind them. Our line bent. Some of their tanks broke through. But our guys behind the line were waiting and not one of those tanks made it back.

scenes.title: Christmas dinner
scenes.narration: Christmas dinner was one can of cold hash, shared between two of us. Lenny said it was the best Christmas dinner of his life. He was lying. So was I, when I agreed with him.

scenes.title: Engines at night
scenes.narration: At night, you could hear their tanks moving out in the dark. Engines starting. Tracks squealing. You never knew where they'd come from next. Lenny would whisper: just listen, Joe. Listen and wait for the morning.

scenes.title: A tank from the south
scenes.narration: The next afternoon, December 26th, a tank came up the road from the south. It was ours. Patton's Third Army had punched through. A thin corridor but a door. The siege of Bastogne was over.

scenes.title: Out of road
scenes.narration: It wasn't the end of the fighting. We stayed in those frozen woods for weeks, and we lost good men there. But at Bastogne, the German offensive ran out of road.

scenes.title: How we held
scenes.narration: So how did we hold Bastogne? Pine branches under us. Bedsheets over us. Soup from a stranger. A friend who rubbed your frozen feet and never stopped talking. And one word from a general who wouldn't quit.

scenes.title: The card
scenes.narration: The newspapers called us the Battered Bastards of Bastogne. We kind of liked it. Lenny got his garage in Texas. And every Christmas for the rest of his life, he sent me a card with one word on it. Nuts.
